message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (Panthera leo) and a zebra (Equus quagga) is the ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria**—the group that contains the orders Carnivora (to which lions belong) and Perissodactyla (to which zebras belong).  

In other words, the two species share a common ancestor that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, when the early Laurasiatherian mammals were diversifying. This ancestor is far older than the last common ancestor of the two species themselves (which would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae), but it is the most recent point at which the lineages leading to lions and zebras diverged.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) are both mammals, but belong to different orders: lions are Carnivora, zebras are Perissodactyla. Their common ancestor would be at the level of the last common ancestor of all placental mammals? Actually, lion and zebra diverged earlier. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the ancestor of the clade Eutheria. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the family Felidae and Equidae, which is the ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lion and zebra would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is the ancestor of the clade that includes Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Cetartiodactyla, Chiroptera, and others. That ancestor lived around 70-80 million years ago. But maybe the question expects "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" or "the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria." Let's think: Lion is in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebra is in order Perissodactyla. Both are Laurasiatheria. The last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria is the ancestor of the clade that includes all those orders. That ancestor would have lived about 70-80 million years ago. So answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a placental mammal that lived ~70-80 million years ago. Alternatively, if we want a more specific taxonomic level: The last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor would be a member of the clade Laurasiatheria. So answer accordingly.
